title: David on the Run and Lying
overview: Running from King Saul, David lies to a priest to get food and a weapon, then escapes danger in an enemy city by pretending to be insane.

parts.label: David arrives alone (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Nob was a town of priests where the main worship tent stood at this time, and the priest is uneasy to see Saul's famous commander show up with no troops. David answers with a made up story about a secret mission for the king, a lie the text reports without excusing.

parts.label: The holy bread (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: The only food was the bread of the Presence, loaves set out before God each week and afterward eaten only by priests, and the priest agrees to share it if David's men have avoided sex, which made a person unfit for holy things for a short time. Jesus later pointed to this story to argue that real human need can come before a religious rule.

parts.label: A watcher at the shrine (v. 7)
parts.note: Doeg, a man from the neighboring land of Edom who managed Saul's herds, is held at the shrine that day, perhaps for a vow or a religious duty; the text does not say why. His presence quietly sets up a deadly outcome in the next chapter.

parts.label: Goliath's sword (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The giant's sword had been kept at the shrine as a trophy, wrapped behind the ephod, a special priestly garment used when seeking God's guidance. David, who won it in battle, takes it gladly, still keeping up his story about the king's urgent errand.

parts.label: Playing mad in Gath (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: David flees to Gath, a Philistine city and Goliath's hometown, where officials recognize him from the victory song and even call him king of the land. Terrified, he fakes insanity by scratching at the gate doors and drooling into his beard, and the disgusted king wants nothing to do with him.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter presents David's deceptions as a failure of trust in God that leads to harm, or as understandable survival tactics for a hunted man that the story does not condemn.
think: When someone is running for their life, where would you draw the line on lying, and who should carry the cost if the lie hurts others?
